contributions.headingText: Clear cell chondrosarcoma is a low-grade malignant cartilaginous neoplasm characterized by lobules of cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, immature woven bone formation, and epiphysial location.
2B50.Z & XH7XB9 Chondrosarcoma of bone and articular cartilage of unspecified sites & Clear cell chondrosarcoma

Approximately two thirds of clear cell chondrosarcomas develop in the femoral and humeral head {31788417; 32297725}. However, tumours have been reported in most bones, including the ribs, skull, spine, hands, and feet.

Signs and symptoms

Pain is the most common presenting symptom: 55% of patients experienced pain for > 1 year; 18% had symptoms for > 5 years {6703199}. Pathological fractures are reported to occur in as many as 26% of cases {32297725}.

Imaging

Radiographically, clear cell chondrosarcoma in the appendicular skeleton presents as a geographical osteolytic lesion extending from the metaphysis into the epiphysis, often exhibiting cartilaginous calcifications {37805864; 31788417; 14530882}. The well-defined margin typically is sclerotic in long bones, but less so in the axial skeleton {31788417; 37805864}. In contrast to chondroblastoma, reactive changes are absent on MRI {14530882}.

Clear cell chondrosarcomas account for approximately 2% of all chondrosarcomas in published case series {2057790; 14530882}; men are almost three times more commonly affected than women. The reported age range is 12–84 years, and the mean age is 40 years {6703199; 10424338; 31788417}, but most patients present in their third to fifth decades of life. Rarely, synchronous tumours have been reported {25289140}.

Cytogenetic analyses of small series have revealed clonal abnormalities, with predominant diploid or near-diploid karyotypes and losses or structural aberrations of chromosome 9 and gain of chromosome 20 {2021921; 7922978; 11793445; 15138578; 16157204}. IDH1/2 variants are absent {21598255; 22674453}. One of 15 clear cell chondrosarcomas investigated for H3.3 variants has shown an H3-3B K37M (K36M) variant, a highly specific driver variant of chondroblastoma, suggesting a potential pathogenetic relation in at least a small subset of tumours {24162739}.
Lesions range from 2 to 13 cm in maximum diameter. They contain soft but gritty material, sometimes with cystic areas. Gross features characteristic of hyaline cartilage can be focal or absent.

The tumours consist of lobules of round to ovoid, large polygonal cells with abundant pale, clear, or slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, which resemble hypertrophic cells of the growth plate {8958302; 16054571}. The cells have distinct cytoplasmic membranes and large round nuclei with mild atypia and central nucleoli. Mitotic figures are rare. Further characteristics frequently observed include regularly distributed woven bone formation with intermingled osteoclast-like giant cells. Areas of conventional low-grade chondrosarcoma with minimally atypical nuclei can be observed in about half of the cases {932066}. The hyaline cartilage can become calcified and/or ossified, which can be detected radiologically as a cartilage-type pattern of mineralization. Areas of cystic degeneration resembling aneurysmal bone cyst can also occur. Infiltrative growth can be seen.

Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemically, the clear cells are often strongly positive for S100 {8958302}. They also show occasional immunoreactivity for cytokeratins (AE1/AE3 and CK18) {22944296}.

Differential diagnosis

The main differential diagnoses include metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma, chondroblastoma, and osteosarcoma. Conventional chondrosarcoma can show areas of clear cell change mimicking clear cell chondrosarcoma and comprising as much as 20% of the tumour volume {31297850}.

Essential: clear cells with abundant cytoplasm and a centrally placed nucleus; presence of woven bone and osteoclast-like giant cells.

Desirable: epiphysial location.
Staging is according to bone sarcoma protocols (see <>TNM staging of tumours of bone). See also the information on staging in section Bone tumours: Introduction.

En bloc resection with clear margins is usually curative. Marginal excision or curettage results in high recurrence rates of as much as 86% {2057790; 6703199}. Metastases, usually to the lungs and other skeletal sites, develop in about 20% of cases, often several years after the initial resection {31788417; 32297725}. The overall mortality rate is about 15% {16239809; 32297725; 31788417}. Dedifferentiation to high-grade sarcoma has been reported in exceptional cases {10935648}.
